learningObjectives: Explain the role of dependencies in Case management
Differentiate between the Case Dependency and Timer wait types
Distinguish between a deliberate Wait Step and a delay caused by awaiting user action

elements.description: An automation shape that deliberately pauses Case processing and resumes it when defined conditions are met. Two Wait types: Case Dependency and Timer. Added to a Process in the Case Life Cycle like any other automation Step.

elements.text: Think of the Wait Step as a red traffic light in the middle of your workflow — it deliberately stops the car (Case) until the condition changes (light turns green). Sitting in traffic waiting for a slow pedestrian to cross is NOT the same — that's a user-action delay, not a red light (Wait Step).

elements.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 190" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Two Wait configurations</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Two Wait configurations</text><g font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)"><text x="30" y="78">Case Dependency → related child status or resolution condition.</text><text x="30" y="110">Timer → configured interval or referenced date/time.</text><text x="30" y="142">An unfinished user Assignment is a different source of delay.</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Use status dependency or time configuration according to what must happen before processing continues.

bulletPoints: Wait Step = deliberate pause in Case processing. Two types: Case Dependency and Timer.
Added to a Process in the Case Life Cycle as an automation shape.

elements.description: Place the Wait Step on the parent. Configure whether any or all children of the selected type must meet the dependency. The related children must already exist when the parent reaches the Step; with no dependent Cases, the flow skips this wait.

A target can be a standard status such as Pending-Approval or an application-defined custom status. The To be resolved option instead waits for a status beginning with Resolved; it does not mean any still-open Case. Configure current-status consideration or subsequent changes as required.
You can allow users to cancel the wait conditions and continue processing the parent Case without waiting for the child to resolve.

elements.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 190" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Case Dependency configuration</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Case Dependency configuration</text><g font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)"><text x="30" y="78">Wait on the parent; children must already exist.</text><text x="30" y="110">Choose any/all children and a standard/custom target status.</text><text x="30" y="142">To be resolved means a Resolved-prefixed status, not an open Case.</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Dependency options include target status, resolution, any/all children, and current or subsequent status consideration.

bulletPoints: Place this dependency wait in the parent workflow.
Configure any versus all dependent children of the selected type.
A standard or custom target status is supported.
To be resolved uses the Resolved status prefix.
Dependent Cases must exist before the parent encounters the Step.
Current versus subsequent status consideration and user cancellation are configurable.

elements.description: Pauses a Case until a time condition is met. Two options: (1) Set date/time interval — pause for a fixed duration (e.g., 24 hours). (2) Reference date/time — pause until a specific date/time stored in a Case field is reached.

items: Fixed interval: a configured 24-hour pause before review.
Reference date: the Case field containing the intended valuation cutoff.
Example duration: a configured 72-hour processing delay; this example is not legal advice or a regulatory requirement.

bulletPoints: Timer option 1: fixed interval — specific hours/minutes.
Timer option 2: reference date/time — pause until a date/time field value is reached.
Choose the interval or date property required by the workflow; do not infer business-calendar support or SLA escalation behavior from Timer alone.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Wait Step vs. User Action Delay

elements.description: A Wait Step is a DELIBERATELY configured automation that pauses Case processing. A user action delay is when Case processing stalls because a user has not completed an Assignment — NOT a Wait Step. These are completely different concepts.

A Case that appears paused because a user hasn't acted on an Assignment or submitted required data. NOT a configured Wait Step — just the natural flow of waiting for human action. Examples: awaiting manager approval, or uploading photos.

elements.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 190" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Configured Wait versus pending Assignment</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Configured Wait versus pending Assignment</text><g font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)"><text x="30" y="78">Wait: execution pauses at the configured condition.</text><text x="30" y="110">Assignment: a user still needs to complete the requested task.</text><text x="30" y="142">A delayed approval alone does not prove that a Wait Step exists.</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Wait Step = intentional process configuration. User action delay = Case waiting on a human — not the same thing.

bulletPoints: Wait Step = deliberate. Configured by SA as an automation shape in the Process.
User action delay = incidental. Case is waiting for a human to complete their Assignment.
Manager not approving = user action delay (NOT Wait Step).
User not submitting photos = user action delay (NOT Wait Step).

examPitfalls.title: Case Dependency Wait Step goes on the PARENT — not the child
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask where the Case Dependency Wait Step is placed. Candidates say 'on the child case.' The Wait Step is placed on the PARENT case — it makes the parent wait until the child case reaches the specified status before continuing.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The Wait Step is added to the PARENT Case. The parent pauses at the Wait Step and waits for the child Case to reach the specified status.

examPitfalls.title: Case Dependency requires a parent-child relationship
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks whether Case Dependency can be used between two unrelated cases. Candidates say yes. Case Dependency Wait Steps require a formal parent-child relationship — unrelated cases cannot use this mechanism.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A hierarchical parent-child Case relationship MUST exist. Case Dependency cannot be used between unrelated Cases.

examPitfalls.title: Custom status targets are supported
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Do not treat To be resolved and Resolved as the only permitted status names, or interpret To be resolved as still open.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A standard or custom target status is allowed. To be resolved instead waits for a status beginning with Resolved.

examPitfalls.title: Waiting for user action is NOT a Wait Step
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question describes a case waiting for a user to complete an Assignment and asks which Wait type is used. Candidates say 'Wait for user action.' Waiting for user action is handled by an Assignment step, not a Wait Step — Wait Steps handle time delays and case dependencies.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A user action delay (manager hasn't approved, user hasn't submitted photos) is NOT a Wait Step — it's a Case waiting for a user to complete an Assignment. A Wait Step is a deliberate, configured automation shape.

examPitfalls.title: Timer has TWO configurations: interval OR reference date
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask how many ways a Timer Wait Step can be configured. Candidates say one (fixed interval). A Timer Wait can be set as a fixed interval (e.g., 3 days from now) OR relative to a date property on the clipboard — both configurations are available.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Timer supports: (1) fixed interval (hours/minutes) and (2) reference date/time — pausing until a specific date/time field value is reached.

examPitfalls.title: Current status and later changes are distinct
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Do not confuse status-timing configuration with the chosen target or the any/all selection.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Consider a child already at the target status when choosing current-status versus later-change behavior. Create children before reaching the dependency Step.

examPitfalls.title: The documented Wait types are Case Dependency and Timer
examPitfalls.trapDescription: User Action and Condition are not extra Wait types in this configuration.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Choose Case Dependency for the described child-status coordination, and Timer for the interval or reference-date pause.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An auto insurance parent Case must pause until the 'Vehicle Damage' child Case is resolved. Which Wait type should the SA configure?

options.text: Case Dependency — pauses the parent Case until the child Case reaches a specified status
Timer — sets a fixed interval for the parent to wait before resuming
Condition — pauses the parent Case until a property value changes
Assignment — routes the parent Case to a manager to confirm child completion

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Use the child-resolution dependency rather than guessing how long that work will take.

optionExplanations.A: Use the child-resolution dependency rather than guessing how long that work will take.
optionExplanations.B: An elapsed interval does not establish that the child has resolved.
optionExplanations.C: Condition is not an additional Wait type in this configuration.
optionExplanations.D: A manager Assignment is not the requested automatic child-status dependency.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is configuring a Case Dependency Wait Step. Where should the Wait Step be added?

options.text: To the parent Case — the parent pauses and waits for the child Case
To the child Case — the child signals the parent when it resolves
To both Cases — both must have matching Wait Steps
To a separate monitoring flow rule that watches both Cases

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The parent needs to pause, so its workflow contains the configured dependency wait.

optionExplanations.A: The parent needs to pause, so its workflow contains the configured dependency wait.
optionExplanations.B: Placing the wait only in the child would pause the wrong workflow.
optionExplanations.C: Matching Wait Steps are not required on both sides of the relationship.
optionExplanations.D: This answer omits the documented parent Wait Step placement.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which statement correctly describes the status or resolution conditions supported by Case Dependency?

options.text: A standard or custom target status is allowed; To be resolved instead waits for a Resolved-prefixed status
Only statuses literally named Completed or Closed are accepted
Custom target statuses are prohibited; only Approved or Rejected are allowed
Every child status change releases the wait regardless of the configured target

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Choose a target status or the resolution option; neither requires the child to remain open.

optionExplanations.A: Choose a target status or the resolution option; neither requires the child to remain open.
optionExplanations.B: These two literal names are not the only allowed target statuses.
optionExplanations.C: The configuration supports application-defined targets rather than prohibiting them.
optionExplanations.D: Only satisfying the selected dependency condition releases the wait, not an arbitrary change.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA wants to use Case Dependency between two Cases that have no parent-child relationship. Is this possible?

options.text: No — Case Dependency requires a hierarchical parent-child relationship
Yes — Case Dependency works between any two Cases in the application
Yes — but only if both Cases are the same Case Type
No — but Timer can be used as a workaround for unrelated Cases

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The described dependency needs a hierarchical Case relationship at runtime.

optionExplanations.A: The described dependency needs a hierarchical Case relationship at runtime.
optionExplanations.B: Merely sharing an application does not establish the required hierarchy.
optionExplanations.C: Sharing a Case Type is not a substitute for the relationship.
optionExplanations.D: A Timer cannot establish that an unrelated Case reached the required status.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A workflow needs a fixed 72-hour pause with no date property or other Cases involved. Which configuration directly expresses that duration?

options.text: Timer — with a fixed interval of 72 hours
Case Dependency — pause until a review child Case reaches 'Resolved'
Case Dependency — configured with a 72-hour timeout on the child Case
Timer — reference a Case field containing a date 72 minutes from now

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The fixed interval directly specifies the requested 72-hour processing delay.

optionExplanations.A: The fixed interval directly specifies the requested 72-hour processing delay.
optionExplanations.B: The question has no child whose resolution should release the wait.
optionExplanations.C: A child dependency is not the requested fixed elapsed interval.
optionExplanations.D: Seventy-two minutes is not the seventy-two-hour requirement, and no reference field is supplied.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Case must resume at the employment verification date/time stored in its field. Which configuration uses that field directly without manually deriving an interval?

options.text: Timer — reference date/time pointing to the employment verification date field
Timer — fixed interval calculated manually to match the verification date
Case Dependency — wait for the verification child Case to reach 'Resolved'
Case Dependency — the verification date field automatically triggers resumption

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The reference uses the supplied date/time property as the resume target.

optionExplanations.A: The reference uses the supplied date/time property as the resume target.
optionExplanations.B: Manually converting the target to an interval does not use the field directly as requested.
optionExplanations.C: The scenario names a date property, not a child-resolution dependency.
optionExplanations.D: A date property alone is not a Case Dependency target status.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An expense report has a pending manager approval Assignment and no configured Wait Step. The manager has not approved it. What explains the delay?

options.text: A user action delay — the Case is waiting for a user to complete an Assignment, not a Wait Step
A Case Dependency Wait Step waiting for the approval child Case
A Timer Wait Step enforcing the approval deadline
Both a user action delay AND a Case Dependency Wait Step simultaneously

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The incomplete human Assignment explains the delay without inventing a Wait Step.

optionExplanations.A: The incomplete human Assignment explains the delay without inventing a Wait Step.
optionExplanations.B: No approval child dependency is configured in this scenario.
optionExplanations.C: No time-based Wait is configured merely because approval is pending.
optionExplanations.D: The scenario explicitly excludes a configured Wait Step.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Collect information Assignment requires accident photos. No Wait Step has been configured and the user has not completed this Assignment. What explains the delay?

options.text: A user action delay — the Case awaits completion of a 'Collect photos' Assignment Step
A Timer Wait Step pausing until the photo upload deadline
A Case Dependency Wait Step waiting for a photo review child Case
A guardrail violation — Cases cannot pause in the Create Stage

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The user still needs to finish the information-collection task.

optionExplanations.A: The user still needs to finish the information-collection task.
optionExplanations.B: An upload deadline Timer is not configured in the supplied workflow.
optionExplanations.C: The question supplies no photo-review child dependency.
optionExplanations.D: An incomplete Assignment is not itself evidence of a guardrail violation.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO are valid Wait types for the Pega Platform Wait Step?

options.text: Case Dependency
Timer
User Action
Condition

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: This is the documented status-based dependency configuration. This is the documented time-based wait configuration.

optionExplanations.A: This is the documented status-based dependency configuration.
optionExplanations.B: This is the documented time-based wait configuration.
optionExplanations.C: Awaiting human completion of an Assignment is not another Wait type.
optionExplanations.D: A condition belongs to configuration logic, not an extra Wait type name here.

practiceQuiz.scenario: The only dependent child is already resolved before its parent reaches a Wait Step configured for resolution. How can the SA include that existing status when evaluating the dependency?

options.text: Configure the Case Dependency Wait Step to consider the child Case's CURRENT status — not just future changes
This is not possible — Case Dependency only watches for future status changes after the parent reaches the Wait Step
Add a second Wait Step to the child Case to re-signal the parent
Switch to a Timer Wait Step — it always evaluates current conditions

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Considering current status covers the already-resolved child without requiring a new status transition.

optionExplanations.A: Considering current status covers the already-resolved child without requiring a new status transition.
optionExplanations.B: This overlooks the available current-status configuration.
optionExplanations.C: A second child wait would not be the direct way to include the existing resolved status.
optionExplanations.D: Timer targets time rather than this child-resolution dependency.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the fundamental difference between a Wait Step and a user action delay?

options.text: A Wait Step is a deliberate process configuration; a user action delay occurs when a user has not completed an Assignment
A Wait Step is configured in Dev Studio; user action delays are configured in App Studio
Wait Steps require SLA configuration; user action delays are handled by escalation rules
Wait Steps are temporary and auto-resolve; user action delays are permanent until manually cleared

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The distinction is the configured dependency or time pause versus unfinished human work.

optionExplanations.A: The distinction is the configured dependency or time pause versus unfinished human work.
optionExplanations.B: The Studio used is not the defining distinction between these sources of delay.
optionExplanations.C: Neither described pause requires the proposed universal SLA setup.
optionExplanations.D: A pending Assignment can finish normally; it is not inherently permanent.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA needs a Case to pause for 30 minutes and then automatically resume. Which is the correct configuration?

options.text: Timer Wait Step with a fixed interval of 30 minutes
Case Dependency Wait Step configured to wait 30 minutes for child Case resolution
An SLA with a 30-minute goal that escalates and resumes the Case
A Condition Wait Step checking if 30 minutes have elapsed

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A fixed 30-minute interval is the direct time-based wait configuration.

optionExplanations.A: A fixed 30-minute interval is the direct time-based wait configuration.
optionExplanations.B: This substitutes child-status dependency for the requested elapsed-time pause.
optionExplanations.C: An SLA goal alone does not define the requested Wait Step and its Timer interval.
optionExplanations.D: Condition is not the documented name of an additional Wait type.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega developer asks about the Case Dependency Wait type. Which TWO statements correctly describe how a Case Dependency Wait works?

options.text: The Case pauses and waits until a specified related Case reaches a defined status or resolution condition
Case Dependency can be used to pause a parent Case until a child Case is resolved or reaches a target status
The Case Dependency Wait type uses a calendar timer to pause for a fixed number of hours or business days
Case Dependency requires an Integration Designer connector to poll the status of the dependent Case

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A configured dependency condition concerns the related child status or resolution. The parent can coordinate with its children using a selected target status or resolution option.

optionExplanations.A: A configured dependency condition concerns the related child status or resolution.
optionExplanations.B: The parent can coordinate with its children using a selected target status or resolution option.
optionExplanations.C: Calendar duration is Timer behavior rather than the status dependency being tested.
optionExplanations.D: The documented parent-child dependency does not require this invented external polling connector.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Claims workflow requires a fixed 48-hour pause before Settlement. Which TWO elements directly implement this time-based pause?

options.text: A Wait Step placed in the process before the Settlement Stage
The Timer wait type configured with a fixed interval of 48 hours
A Case Dependency wait type targeting the status of a related external Case
An SLA deadline alone, with no configured Wait Step

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the actual dependency, its configuration and when it is evaluated.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Place the deliberate pause in the workflow before the work that must wait. The Timer interval directly expresses the fixed forty-eight-hour requirement.

optionExplanations.A: Place the deliberate pause in the workflow before the work that must wait.
optionExplanations.B: The Timer interval directly expresses the fixed forty-eight-hour requirement.
optionExplanations.C: The condition here concerns elapsed time, not another Case reaching a status.
optionExplanations.D: A deadline alone is not a deliberate workflow pause with a Timer interval.

quickRecap.value: Deliberate automation shape that pauses Case processing. Two types: Case Dependency and Timer.
The parent waits for any/all configured children to reach a selected status or resolve. Consider current versus subsequent status behavior.
Pauses Case for: (1) fixed interval (hours/min), OR (2) until a reference date/time field value is reached.

Wait Step = deliberate SA configuration. User action delay = Case waiting for user to complete an Assignment. These are DIFFERENT — manager not approving and user not submitting photos are NOT Wait Steps.
A hierarchy must exist and dependent Cases must already be created; otherwise the wait is skipped.
Standard and custom target statuses are supported. To be resolved uses the Resolved status prefix.
You can allow users to cancel the wait conditions and continue processing without waiting for the child Case.
